prompt: Which of these statements are **true**? Select all that apply. (n is the input size; T(n) is the number of steps the algorithm takes on an input of size n; O(...) is an upper bound on growth.)

options.text: If each step touches O(1) memory cells, O(T(n)) time can touch at most O(T(n)) auxiliary cells, excluding input storage
options.explanation: True under the stated model. This does not bound untouched virtual address space reserved in bulk.

options.text: An algorithm using O(n) bits can still take exponential time
options.explanation: True. An n-bit counter reuses its storage while enumerating every bit pattern; n is bit count.

options.text: The stack space used by a recursive function equals its total number of calls
options.explanation: False. Space depends on the maximum number of frames alive *at once* (the depth), not on the total. Naive fib makes exponentially many calls with linear depth.

options.text: Recursive binary search on index bounds uses O(log n) stack space
options.explanation: True. Halving the range on each call gives logarithmic stack depth; n is the original item count. An iterative version uses O(1).

options.text: Standard array merge sort is in place because its recursion stack is only O(log n) deep
options.explanation: False. The stack is O(log n), but the merge step needs an O(n) temporary buffer, so its auxiliary space is O(n). Here n is the input size or recursive argument stated in the question.

workedExample: A constant number of cell touches per step bounds newly touched auxiliary cells by total steps, excluding stored input and untouched reservations. Small reusable storage can support very long computations. Recursive space counts the deepest live chain plus retained buffers: binary search has logarithmic depth, while merge sort also needs a linear merge buffer.
